1	# core
2	
3	Claudinite's own surface in a repo that runs it: the vendored mount, the declaration that activates a
4	pack, adopting Claudinite and adopting a pack, and the contract every scheduled task is written to.
5	
6	**Mandatory.** `basics` `requires` this pack, so the closure vendors its content and materializes its
7	declaration wherever a declaration is written; the one-time `core-seed` migration record declares it
8	into members that already exist. Removing the entry is not an opt-out — it is drift, and `claudinite-lifecycle-declared`
9	reports it.
10	
11	## Rules (`RULES.md`)
12	
13	| Rule | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
14	|---|---|---|---|
15	| Reading a rule that arrived from Claudinite | high | correctness | prose: 43 words + check (`claudinite-isolation`) |
16	| Finding a mounted skill's real path | medium | complexity | prose: 81 words |
17	| Wanting a pack's rules to apply here | high | correctness | prose: 47 words + check (`claudinite-lifecycle-declared`) |
18	| Renaming or removing a pack's declaration | high | correctness | prose: 73 words |
19	| Adding a pack | medium | complexity | prose: 27 words |
20	| Setting a project up on Claudinite | medium | complexity | prose: 15 words |
21	| Deciding which pack owns a lesson | medium | complexity | prose: 59 words |
22	| Judging whether Claudinite is current here | medium | correctness | prose: 51 words |
23	| Answering "why did the mount not update" | medium | correctness | prose: 39 words |
24	
25	## Checks
26	
27	Each of these asks the same kind of question: **is Claudinite working in this repo** — declared,
28	converged, gated, scheduled. A repo can fail any of them silently, which is why they are checks and
29	not prose: the session that has lost its rules is the session least able to notice.
30	
31	| Check | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
32	|---|---|---|---|
33	| `claudinite-lifecycle-declared` | critical | correctness | check: blocking |
34	| `rules-index-current` | critical | correctness | check: blocking |
35	| `claudinite-isolation` | high | complexity | check: blocking |
36	| `conformance-workflow` | high | correctness | check: advisory |
37	| `conformance-work-scope` | high | correctness | check: advisory |
38	| `scheduler-workflow-shape` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
39	| `legacy-shape-in-use` | medium | complexity | check: advisory |
40	| `skill-loaded-before-editing` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
41	| `skills-index-current` | medium | correctness | check: blocking |
42	
43	What goes wrong when one fires:
44	
45	- `claudinite-lifecycle-declared` — this pack's entry is gone from `.claudinite-settings.json`, so none of the rules above run and the session cannot tell.
46	- `rules-index-current` — the generated index is missing, stale or unimported: the repo's packs contribute no prose to any session.
47	- `claudinite-isolation` — the repo's own code reaches into `.claudinite/`, so the next canon refactor is a breaking migration for code the canon does not own (a declared `forbidReferences` barrier edge).
48	- `conformance-workflow` — nothing in CI runs the world sweep unfiltered on a pull request, so conformance is ungated and the maintenance PR never lands.
49	- `conformance-work-scope` — CI gates the tree but not the change, so every commit-scoped rule is enforced only where a session's Stop hook happens to run.
50	- `scheduler-workflow-shape` — the vendored scheduler's cron, concurrency or dispatch guard has drifted: staggering, double-run safety or manual runs break.
51	
52	The **task contract** and its checks are deliberately NOT here. Those ask whether a task is
53	*written* correctly, which is authoring; every check above asks whether Claudinite is *working* in
54	this repo. They live with the rest of the authoring surface.
55	
56	The scope cuts the other way too: a rule about how the **canon's own** content is maintained is not
57	this pack's, however much it looks like one. `catalog-completeness` — `packs/README.md` lists every
58	`packs/<name>/` — reads as Claudinite machinery and is not: it can only fire in the corpus repo, and
59	what it guards is a hand-maintained index, not a member's status. It stays with the other
60	doc-integrity rules.
61	
62	`skill-loaded-before-editing` is the Stop-time half of **path-scoped skills**: a skill names
63	the files it must be loaded for under `force-load-on-file-edits-paths` in its SKILL.md frontmatter
64	`metadata` (the harness's own `paths` is a limiter on when it offers a skill, so it cannot carry
65	this), the engine's PreToolUse guard holds a file tool aimed there until the session has
66	loaded that skill, and this rule catches the edits the guard never saw (a `sed`, a heredoc) by
67	asking the diff the same question. Both read one resolver,
68	`engine/pack_loader/path-scoped-skills.mjs`. A load is a `Skill` tool call or a `Read` of the
69	skill's own SKILL.md. `skills-index-current` keeps the generated
70	`.claudinite/claudinite-skills.GENERATED.md` — every mounted skill with what loads it, the
71	scoped ones first — naming what the declared packs actually bundle.
72	
73	## Skills
74	
75	| Skill | For |
76	|---|---|
77	| [`adopt-claudinite`](skills/adopt-claudinite/SKILL.md) | setting a project up on Claudinite for the first time — mount, hooks, checks, skills — and re-baselining one to pick up updates |
78	| [`adopt-pack`](skills/adopt-pack/SKILL.md) | adding a pack to a repo that already runs Claudinite: declare, interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land |
79	
80	The adoption skills bundle two more checks of the same kind, over the answers a member stores
81	against each declared pack's questions:
82	
83	| Check | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
84	|---|---|---|---|
85	| `adoption-answers-pending` | medium | complexity | check: blocking |
86	| `interview-answer-stale` | low | complexity | check: advisory |
87	
88	## Tasks
89	
90	| Task | frequency | Runs when |
91	|---|---|---|
92	| `update` | daily (02:00 anchor) | the mount is behind the canon, or a declared pack moved |
93	| `adopt-requested-packs` | daily | the repo carries an open pack-adoption request |
94	
95	`update` is the per-repo self-refresh — the task that converges a member's mount and stamps it. It
96	is why `claudinite-lifecycle-declared` is blocking: a member runs `update` from its **vendored** copy, and
97	`discoverTasks` finds only a literally-declared pack's tasks, so a repo that loses this pack's entry
98	loses its self-refresh, and nothing is left that could deliver it one. That is also why the task
99	arrived here a change later than the rest of the pack — it moved only once every non-dormant member's
100	declaration had been read back and confirmed to carry `core`.

10	  (e.g. `.claude/skills/<name>/`) that holds only that one `SKILL.md`, any relative link the
11	  skill's own text carries (to a sibling doc, a sibling skill) was written for its real home and
12	  dangles from that announced base — resolve such links against the canon path instead.
13	
14	- **Wanting a pack's rules to apply here** — declare its id in `.claudinite-settings.json`. Nothing
15	  activates by being mounted, fingerprinted or present on disk, so a pack whose files you can see
16	  but whose id is undeclared contributes no prose, no checks, no skills and no tasks.
17	
18	- **Renaming or removing a pack's declaration** — re-run
19	  `node .claudinite/shared/engine/converge-wiring.mjs <owner/repo> --badges` in the same
20	  change. The README's `<!-- claudinite:packs -->` badge row is a one-time seed the update flow

The baseline pack — the `RULES.md` prose every session loads (injected by the pack-prose hook) plus the working-discipline checks. Its subject is **how work is done**, whatever tool is running it. Declared explicitly like every other pack — no pack is active by default; bootstrap seeds the declaration and the nightly baselining backfills it into existing consumers.

1	# iOS
2	
3	- **The agent's own sandbox has no macOS and no Swift toolchain — every Swift/iOS change is
4	  verified by CI alone.** The toolchain isn't merely absent from the image; the download is
5	  typically blocked by the sandbox's own network policy, not just missing. Nothing Swift-side
6	  compiles or runs locally in an agent session, so budget confidence accordingly: a Swift/iOS
7	  change is "verified" only once the macOS CI runner reports on it, never before.
8	
9	- **An Apple Developer Documentation page is JS-rendered — a plain fetch returns only the page
10	  title.** Fetch the JSON mirror instead: `developer.apple.com/tutorials/data/documentation/…`
11	  (same path as the HTML page, under `tutorials/data/`) carries the actual content.

1	# Working discipline
2	
3	- **Starting any requested change** — begin from the *problem*, not the solution, in any
4	  repository and not just this one. Reach an explicit shared understanding with the owner of the
5	  problem the change is meant to solve **and** agreement that the requested change is the best way
6	  to solve it; a different fix, or none, may serve better.
7	
8	- **Replying to an owner comment** — open with an explicit classification line,
9	  `Comment class: correction | feature | process-change | other`, where `other` covers questions,
10	  approvals and command phrases and a mixed comment names each part. An automation dispatch prompt
11	  is a comment too: class `other`, in your *first* substantive reply rather than at the end of the
12	  run. Put the class **alone on the line** and any explanation on the next one: the line is scanned
13	  for *every* class token on it, so restating the menu declares all of them. A class cannot be taken
14	  back, and a clean re-declaration further down does not override the first.
15	
16	- **Acting on a correction** — you misunderstood something. Repair the shared understanding, then
17	  rework what the misread already touched; the artifact changes as much as the correction demands,
18	  but a correction never adds a new requirement or rule.
19	
20	- **Acting on a feature** — agree on the requirement, record it in the project's requirements
21	  document (its executable spec, where it keeps one), write the test that proves it and watch it
22	  fail, then implement until it passes.
23	
24	- **Acting on a process change** — the owner is changing *how* work is done. Land it as durable
25	  rules in the project's local scope, its own local packs (in Claudinite itself, its packs), routed
26	  through the mechanism promotion ladder (platform setting → hook → check → skill → prose).
27	  Promoting a rule into the shared canon is the growth lifecycle's separate call, not the
28	  interactive session's.
29	
30	- **Choosing what goes on that ladder** — only a rule that constrains *how work is done* and
31	  outlives any one feature; a checkable signature doesn't earn a rule its place. Reject two shapes
32	  outright: a check that asserts particular code exists or still reads a particular way (it pins a
33	  point in time), and a rule derivable from the product's requirements (that is a requirement —
34	  take it to the feature path, the requirements document and the test that proves it).
35	
36	- **Landing a rule anywhere on the ladder** — author the assurance first, the check the future
37	  world must satisfy, execute it and watch it fail, and only then make the fixes that turn it green.
38	  At the prose rung, where no check can carry an in-flight judgment rule, the equivalent step is
39	  showing the corpus doesn't already cover the rule before writing it.
40	
41	- **Building a mechanism for a behavior** — verify against a real run that it isn't already
42	  provided.
43	
44	- **Building release, deploy, versioning or CI plumbing** — look for the shared pack that owns it
45	  first; copying a mechanic from a sibling repo is the tell that it belongs centrally. If no pack
46	  owns it, report the gap rather than author a third copy.
47	
48	- **Finishing a change** — watch it work **now**; never park it on "check tomorrow". What a task
49	  costs is its shelf-life, the time from starting it until everyone can forget about it.
50	
51	- **Changing scheduled or unattended machinery** — force a run now (the scheduler's wake lever, a
52	  `workflow_dispatch`, the fleet-wide force sweep) and watch it to a terminal state rather than wait
53	  for its next natural run.
54	
55	- **Planning a migration** — prefer the design that converges in one forced pass to the one that
56	  trickles across nightly cycles, accept legacy input at the door so nothing has to wait for
57	  stragglers, and drive the stragglers with a standing mechanism rather than a phase someone must
58	  remember to close. Write every phase's code — the cleanup, the destructive tail and every
59	  legacy tolerance's removal included — before asking for approval, and chain each execution step
60	  to the verification of the one before it rather than to anyone's memory;
61	  [writing-migration-plans](skills/writing-migration-plans/SKILL.md) owns that ordering and the
62	  chain's mechanics.
63	
64	- **Adding a legacy tolerance** (a dual read, an accepted old spelling, a shim) — it is
65	  scaffolding, not a feature: ship it with an advisory that fires where the old shape is still in
66	  use, and with its removal already a link in the migration's chain, due one stated convergence
67	  window after that advisory reaches the holders. (2)
68	
69	- **Choosing an automerge policy for a PR or a chain link** — write it as a prediction of the
70	  change's shape, the folders and kinds you expect the diff to touch, and never widen it to fit the
71	  diff that arrived: a policy that fails is the speed bump that puts a person back on the trail,
72	  not an error to route around. (1)
73	
74	- **Predicting a change that could delete production data or degrade the experience past what a
75	  later PR undoes** — its policy is `nothing`, whatever its diff class; irreversibility is the
76	  first of the two things review here exists to catch. (1)
77	
78	- **Handing over a change whose diff reached more folders or files than its request implied** —
79	  say so, and name the abstraction that would have kept it in one place: the reviewer reads which
80	  folders moved to judge whether the change made sense, and a wide diff for a small ask is the
81	  growth lesson review is for, not a defect. (1)
82	
83	- **Retiring a system by folding its function into another** — verify the *machinery* came over,
84	  not just its historical output: a copied directory of the old system's artifacts visually
85	  launders the absence of the live generator that produced them, so audit for the generator
86	  explicitly, in the same pass, rather than inferring it from the presence of past output. And
87	  before dropping a carried-over aggregate on the assumption "the next run recomputes it," check
88	  whether the new generator's own inputs retain the same history the aggregate already holds — a
89	  stateless recompute over inputs the new system keeps only for a bounded window starts the series
90	  shorter than a file carried over from elsewhere already carries.
91	
92	- **When verifying now is genuinely impossible** (an external release window, an upstream fix in
93	  flight, an effect that only appears once the change is deployed, converged or loaded by a later
94	  session) — the follow-up is a mechanism that comes to you, never a human's memory and never an
95	  offer to the owner to go and check later. File it with
96	  [verify-in-production](skills/verify-in-production/SKILL.md), unasked, **once the PR has
97	  merged** and never before — a PR can be rejected, and a still-open branch can be rewritten
98	  under you, either of which strands a verification whose premise never reached `main`. The
99	  skill owns both halves — whether this change needs one at all (most don't; a test that ran is
100	  already the mechanism), and the issue that states what puts the change in production and what
101	  proves it works there.
102	
103	- **Finishing a larger element** — one that earned a design doc or a phased tracking issue — a
104	  point verification is not enough: schedule the review that comes back once the element has
105	  lived in production about a week, asking whether it is working, misused, overused or underused
106	  against its real record — with the brief written at design time, expected amounts, signals and
107	  the metrics that measure them included, never improvised when the review runs.
108	  [production-retrospective](skills/production-retrospective/SKILL.md) owns the trigger, the
109	  brief, and the lane's other classes — canon, local-pack and fleet alike.
110	
111	- **Receiving feedback that flags a misunderstanding** — check whether the artifact is already
112	  correct before expanding it; if it is, say so and push back rather than edit.
113

20	- **Nothing you post to a tracker can be edited — resolve every value before the comment goes up.** The GitHub toolsets these runs use offer comment *creation* and no comment-update tool, so a comment that goes out wrong can only be appended to, leaving the wrong value and its correction both standing forever. An agent session also has **no ambient clock**: a timestamp is only true if you read it (one shell call) rather than filling a placeholder you mean to fix later. Same for every PR number, sha and label a comment asserts — resolve, then post.
21	- **When the outcome your ceiling names is mechanically unavailable, stop short and say so — never substitute a riskier action to close the gap.** A routine told to land work through an auto-merging PR cannot when the repository has auto-merge disabled and its checks will not conclude. The gap looks one command wide, and improvising a merge to close it costs more than the unlanded change does. Where a shared delivery procedure exists (Claudinite's `packs/claudinite-tasks/deliver-pr.md`), the merges it licenses — like the direct merge on a base branch that requires nothing, where the arm is rejected "clean status" by design — are the sanctioned path, not a workaround; anything outside them stays unlanded. An open PR plus a plain statement of what could not be armed and why is a complete, honest result. Re-try the mechanism on each run rather than assuming either state is permanent, and drop the workaround the moment it succeeds.
22	- **A change-gated routine must exclude its *own* writes from its triggers, or it feeds itself.** A routine that commits to, files issues in, or emits artifacts into the same repos it monitors will re-fire on its own output unless every trigger filters it out: its own maintenance commits must not count as "the project changed" (match them by bot-author / `[skip ci]` / a subject convention and exclude — and keep that matcher current with the wording the routine actually writes, or a near-miss silently reads as real work); its own standing-tracker/issue updates must not count as activity (a tracker rewritten every run always sits inside a fixed lookback window, so it re-triggers forever); its own generated plan/report artifact must not count as a repo change. The tell is a routine that fires every cycle on a fleet that is actually quiet. Treat "the routine's inputs never include the routine's outputs" as an invariant when wiring any change-detection signal.
23	- When an unattended routine takes an **irreversible or outward-facing action** (closing an issue, deleting a branch, sending a message), the spec must **define the trigger condition concretely and default to the safe path** — not just name the action. A bare "close if done" invites a wrong close on a superficial match; "close *only* when the ask is verifiably true of the target's current state — else comment" cannot. State what counts as the condition and where to verify it, and make the reversible option (leave it, comment, escalate) the default whenever the check is inconclusive.
24	- A `[Merge Without Review]` security warning on a task's own unattended merge is expected, not a finding to escalate — adjudicate it in one step. When a task's declared delivery policy is auto-merge and its target's checks require no human approval (or the arm is rejected `clean status` and a direct merge is the sanctioned path), the harness still flags the completion with a security warning because no human approval appears in the transcript — that is the harness reporting the *shape* of the action, not evaluating whether it was licensed. Confirm the task's declared delivery policy and its outcome ceiling permit the merge, then converge normally; escalating every occurrence to human review would wedge a routine that is designed to merge unattended.
25	<<<<<<< HEAD
26	- A background subagent dispatch shares the parent's working directory unless isolated, so the parent's own end-of-session checks can misread the subagent's activity as its own. Without `isolation: "worktree"`, a background agent runs in the *same* checkout as the session that spawned it, so while it's running: its uncommitted WIP can look like the parent's own dirty diff to a git-status-based finding, and if it switches branches (e.g. checking out another branch to inspect or fix it), a check that reads the current branch now reads *its* branch, not the parent's. Before diagnosing such a finding as your own — one naming "the branch" or "the commit", or unreferenced/uncommitted changes — check whether a background agent is still running; if a mid-dispatch finding names a branch other than the one you were assigned, switch back to your own branch to clear it rather than treating the finding as real.
27	- **Before concluding a subagent whose handle went unreachable left no progress, check every place its output could have landed — not just git state and the dispatch's own PR comments.** A subagent that hits something worth escalating may record that as a filed tracker issue rather than a commit; a recovery check that reads only local git log and the dispatch PR's comments can miss it entirely, read "nothing survived," and relaunch a duplicate investigation that reproduces — and re-files — the same finding.

Before diagnosing such a finding as your own — one naming "the branch" or "the commit", or unreferenced/uncommitted changes — check whether a background agent is still running; if a mid-dispatch finding names a branch other than the one you were assigned, switch back to your own branch to clear it rather than treating the finding as real. Never amend a subagent's already-pushed commit, and never relay a "fix" instruction built around a check that doesn't exist as described — both act on a misdiagnosis instead of correcting it. And if switching back (or an amend) is itself refused by the environment's own permission classifier, don't retry or force it: a live subagent is still using the shared checkout, and the branch — and the false-positive noise with it — reverts to yours on its own the moment the subagent finishes.
30	- **A lost subagent's handle going unreachable is not evidence it made no progress — check every channel it could have written to, not just git.** A subagent whose process is interrupted or restarted mid-task can have already produced real output through a side channel (filing a tracking issue, say) moments before going silent. A recovery check that reads only git log/status and a dispatch PR's own comments will read that as "nothing survived" and relaunch a fresh subagent from a from-scratch briefing — which re-investigates the same ground and produces a duplicate. Before asserting "no progress" in a relaunch briefing, also search for anything the lost subagent may have filed (issues, comments), not just commits.
31	- **Don't perform a dispatched subagent's work yourself before its result is actually in hand.** Backgrounding a subagent to do X and then, before its completion notification (or your own scheduled wakeup) arrives, independently doing X yourself makes the subagent's run entirely redundant the moment it does report back. Once you've stated a wait-for-subagent plan, actually wait — check what its notification says before taking the action it was dispatched to take.

33	- **Parallel background agents that each dump external content to disk need a collision-proof filename, not a shared generic one.** Subagents dispatched from one session share its scratchpad directory, so a fleet of them each told (or defaulting) to write the same generic path — a bare `log.jsonl`, `out.txt` — race on it: one agent's write can land mid-read by another, producing a truncated or mixed-content file with no error from either side. Give each agent's output a name that can't collide with its siblings' — the source item's own filename, or the agent's own session id — never a shared default.

Without `isolation: "worktree"`, a background agent runs in the *same* checkout as the session that spawned it, so while it's running: its uncommitted WIP can look like the parent's own dirty diff to a git-status-based finding, and if it switches branches (e.g. checking out another branch to inspect or fix it), a check that reads the current branch now reads *its* branch, not the parent's. Before diagnosing such a finding as your own — one naming "the branch" or "the commit", or unreferenced/uncommitted changes — check whether a background agent is still running; if a mid-dispatch finding names a branch other than the one you were assigned, switch back to your own branch to clear it rather than treating the finding as real. Never amend a subagent's already-pushed commit, and never relay a "fix" instruction built around a check that doesn't exist as described — both act on a misdiagnosis instead of correcting it. And if switching back (or an amend) is itself refused by the environment's own permission classifier, don't retry or force it: a live subagent is still using the shared checkout, and the branch — and the false-positive noise with it — reverts to yours on its own the moment the subagent finishes.
- **Before concluding a subagent whose handle went unreachable left no progress, check every place its output could have landed — not just git state and the dispatch's own PR comments.** A subagent that hits something worth escalating may record that as a filed tracker issue rather than a commit; a recovery check that reads only local git log and the dispatch PR's comments can miss it entirely, read "nothing survived," and relaunch a duplicate investigation that reproduces — and re-files — the same finding.
- **A lost subagent's handle going unreachable is not evidence it made no progress — check every channel it could have written to, not just git.** A subagent whose process is interrupted or restarted mid-task can have already produced real output through a side channel (filing a tracking issue, say) moments before going silent. A recovery check that reads only git log/status and a dispatch PR's own comments will read that as "nothing survived" and relaunch a fresh subagent from a from-scratch briefing — which re-investigates the same ground and produces a duplicate. Before asserting "no progress" in a relaunch briefing, also search for anything the lost subagent may have filed (issues, comments), not just commits.
- **Don't perform a dispatched subagent's work yourself before its result is actually in hand.** Backgrounding a subagent to do X and then, before its completion notification (or your own scheduled wakeup) arrives, independently doing X yourself makes the subagent's run entirely redundant the moment it does report back. Once you've stated a wait-for-subagent plan, actually wait — check what its notification says before taking the action it was dispatched to take.

lines: - **A change-gated routine must exclude its *own* writes from its triggers, or it feeds itself.** A routine that commits to, files issues in, or emits artifacts into the same repos it monitors will re-fire on its own output unless every trigger filters it out: its own maintenance commits must not count as "the project changed" (match them by bot-author / `[skip ci]` / a subject convention and exclude — and keep that matcher current with the wording the routine actually writes, or a near-miss silently reads as real work); its own standing-tracker/issue updates must not count as activity (a tracker rewritten every run always sits inside a fixed lookback window, so it re-triggers forever); its own generated plan/report artifact must not count as a repo change. The tell is a routine that fires every cycle on a fleet that is actually quiet. Treat "the routine's inputs never include the routine's outputs" as an invariant when wiring any change-detection signal.

- When an unattended routine takes an **irreversible or outward-facing action** (closing an issue, deleting a branch, sending a message), the spec must **define the trigger condition concretely and default to the safe path** — not just name the action. A bare "close if done" invites a wrong close on a superficial match; "close *only* when the ask is verifiably true of the target's current state — else comment" cannot. State what counts as the condition and where to verify it, and make the reversible option (leave it, comment, escalate) the default whenever the check is inconclusive.

- A `[Merge Without Review]` security warning on a task's own unattended merge is expected, not a finding to escalate — adjudicate it in one step. When a task's declared delivery policy is auto-merge and its target's checks require no human approval (or the arm is rejected `clean status` and a direct merge is the sanctioned path), the harness still flags the completion with a security warning because no human approval appears in the transcript — that is the harness reporting the *shape* of the action, not evaluating whether it was licensed. Confirm the task's declared delivery policy and its outcome ceiling permit the merge, then converge normally; escalating every occurrence to human review would wedge a routine that is designed to merge unattended.

- **Parallel background agents that each dump external content to disk need a collision-proof filename, not a shared generic one.** Subagents dispatched from one session share its scratchpad directory, so a fleet of them each told (or defaulting) to write the same generic path — a bare `log.jsonl`, `out.txt` — race on it: one agent's write can land mid-read by another, producing a truncated or mixed-content file with no error from either side. 195	## `commit.gpgsign = true` does not cover merge commits
196	
197	`commit.gpgsign = true` signs ordinary commits but does not apply to `git merge` — each merge produces an unsigned commit even with signing fully configured. In a repo that enforces commit verification, this requires a fix-up after the fact. Cover merges proactively: either pass `-S` to every `git merge` call, or set `merge.gpgsign = true` globally so merges are signed the same way commits are.
198	
199	## When access is scoped to an explicit repo list, query per-repo — never an org/user-wide search
200	
201	A broad call (e.g. `search_repositories` with `org:X`, or any list/search tool that takes no repo argument) returns every repo the token can see, not just an allowed subset — filtering the result afterward doesn't undo the fact that disallowed repos' data was already pulled into the call. When operating under a repo allowlist, scope every call explicitly instead: pass the specific `owner`/`repo` params, or anchor the query to `repo:owner/name`, one call per repo in the allowlist rather than one broad call filtered after the fact.
202	
203	<<<<<<< HEAD
204	A session scoped to a **single** repo hits the same boundary from the other side: a call naming a *different* repo is denied outright, not merely filtered. Before spending a call rediscovering that denial, check what repo the session is actually scoped to — and look for the answer in what you already have. An issue or PR body that references the other repo often already carries its own self-description of the state you were about to go fetch.
205	
206	## `search_code`'s index can lag — don't trust it alone to enumerate a population
207	
208	Reconnaissance across many repos (which ones reference X, which ones need a given change) often reaches for `search_code`, but its index is not the source of truth for coverage: it can silently undercount, missing repos that genuinely match. Where you have a way to enumerate the true candidate set directly — fetching each candidate's own file, walking a known roster — cross-check `search_code`'s result against that before trusting it as complete; one fleet-wide sweep found only 3 of 11 actually-affected repos through `search_code` alone.
209	=======
210	## Write access scoped to one repo doesn't license routing around the boundary for a fix that belongs elsewhere
211	
212	A session's push/write access is commonly scoped to a single repo, even when it can *read* others (a cloned dependency, a monorepo neighbour, an upstream project). Finding a genuine bug in a repo you can only read is not license to hunt for a way to push there anyway — that scoping is a deliberate boundary, not an oversight to route around, and it doesn't move for a good reason. Finish and verify the fix in a scratch clone of the repo that owns it, then attach it as a diff/patch to an issue in the repo you *can* write to, carrying what you verified — so a session with the right scope can `git apply` it and land it properly reviewed.
213	>>>>>>> ae51de60 (Promote lessons from ClaudiniteWebsite, EdFringeNow, TLDR, WIP)
214	
215	## Cap *and* qualify every list/search call — an unbounded one blows the tool-result limit
216	
217	A list or search API call that isn't bounded returns a full page of full-bodied records and overruns the agent's tool-result cap, which costs two or three further calls to dig the answer back out of the spilled result — a pure-overhead round trip on a call whose wanted answer was a single record. Two independent bounds, both needed:
218	
219	- **Qualify the query so it matches what you mean.** A bare string handed to an issue/PR search is a *full-text* search over the whole repo — title, body, and comments — so a lookup for one known issue returns every issue that merely mentions the phrase, each with its whole body. Anchor it to the field (`in:title "<exact title>"`), or use the narrower tool (a label-filtered `list_issues`, a run-id or head-SHA query) instead of a search.

2	name: unattended-agents
3	description: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
4	---
5	
6	# Agent architecture principles
7	
8	- An agent invoked **unattended** by automation (a CI workflow, not interactive Claude Code) should be left only the part of the task that genuinely needs its judgment; hard-code every deterministic part — the setup before *and* the wrap-up after — in the workflow around it. A step described in prose is one the agent can skip, reorder, or improvise; a step the workflow runs in code can't be fumbled, and the shorter prompt keeps the agent on the one thing only it can do. Push that boundary continually: each time a step proves mechanical, move it out of the prompt and into the workflow.
9	- When a routine needs a capability its own runtime lacks — a credential spanning more repos than the session's allowlist, an execution surface the sandbox can't reach — wrap that part as a **dispatch-only executor** (e.g. a `workflow_dispatch`-only GitHub Actions workflow holding the privileged token) that the routine triggers and awaits. The executor carries **no schedule of its own**: give it a cron and it silently becomes a second orchestrator with a competing trigger. One schedule, owned by the orchestrating routine; executors run only when dispatched. State only the executor's *contract* in the routine's prose (what it computes, what the agent may rely on) — its internal rules live in its code, unlike validators of the agent's *own* output, which the prose must still teach (see the routine-folder rules below).
10	- **The routine's own in-session steps reach GitHub through the session's MCP tools — never a REST client or a `GITHUB_TOKEN`.** This is the corollary of the rule above: the steps a routine runs *itself* operate over the repos the session was granted, which the MCP GitHub tools already cover, so they need no token. A REST client, a raw `api.github.com` `fetch`, or a `process.env.GITHUB_TOKEN` read in in-session code (a migration pass, an agent-stage worker doc's steps) is the tell that the step was mis-built as if it were the CI *executor* — and it will 401 in the MCP-only session it's scheduled in, silently turning the run into a no-op. Only the part that genuinely needs the broader credential moves to a dispatch-only executor; everything else is MCP. *Diagnosing* whether in-session code can reach a host: probe with a tool that honors the sandbox's `HTTPS_PROXY` — `curl` does — never a bare `node -e "fetch(...)"`, whose global `fetch` ignores `HTTPS_PROXY` and goes **direct**, returning a verdict that bypasses (and so misreports) the proxy's real one.
11	- Size a routine spec at checklist altitude, and re-compress after every scope addition — specs bloat by accretion, not by any one edit. Keep it to terse imperative bullets stating outcomes, bounds, and judgment criteria; a delegated step gets its contract only, procedure another doc owns gets a pointer (never a restatement), and a why-clause earns its place only where the rule is surprising. Symptoms you've absorbed what belongs elsewhere: the spec re-explains a companion script's logic or a sibling doc's steps, or has grown to several times its sibling routines (the house norm is ~40–90 lines).
12	- Bound an unattended agent's **write surface**, and enforce it from outside the agent. Pre-create the exact file(s) it may edit, tell it to touch nothing else (no new files, no edits to shared code it might be tempted to "improve"), and after it stops, verify the diff in the workflow — reverting anything outside the allowed set rather than trusting the prompt. Prose is a request; the post-hoc diff check is the guarantee, so a misbehaving agent's blast radius is bounded no matter how it strays. Anything the agent would otherwise reach into belongs inlined in its own file (as a source's local helper), not edited in place.
13	- In a multi-stage unattended pipeline, converge **every** failure exit — including an infrastructure failure in a pre-agent setup stage (a fetch, an auth step, scaffolding) — to the same human-triage state as an agent-detected failure. A setup-phase failure that reports itself but leaves the original trigger untouched (e.g. a label still set) makes the item look unprocessed rather than blocked, silently defeating the escalation path. Treat every failure mode as equivalent from the triage perspective.
14	- An unattended agent must **never invoke a tool that surfaces a blocking approval it cannot answer** — there is no human present to click "Allow," so the run stalls indefinitely on step one. The multi-agent-orchestration **Workflow tool is the classic trap**: it mandates an interactive opt-in on *every* run (the prompt only disappears under bypass-permissions / headless modes you cannot rely on the scheduler being in), so a routine that fans out through it hangs before doing any work. Fan out with **plain subagent dispatch** (the Agent/Task tool) instead — it carries no such gate and the orchestrator honors any phase barriers itself — and reserve the Workflow tool for interactive sessions where a human can consent. The general rule: an unattended agent's whole tool path must be answer-free.
15	- **Dispatch a subagent under worktree isolation whenever it may commit.** Without it the child works in the parent's checkout and leaves it wherever it finished — on the child's branch — so the parent's branch-scoped end-of-session checks judge the *child's* commits against the *parent's* transcript and file findings the parent cannot act on. Pass the isolation flag on the dispatch (`isolation: "worktree"`); recovering after the fact means checking the parent back onto its own assigned branch and re-verifying everything.
16	- **A routine that correctly declines has not failed — converge failures, not declines.** When the item a run was dispatched for genuinely cannot be processed (an unreachable source, a dead link, an empty result), record the reason on that item, mark it for human attention, and exit **zero**. Failing the task instead raises a *second* human-triage signal for the same item and reports the pipeline as broken when it in fact judged correctly. Partial success is the same shape: the items that did process still land.
17	- **A run that *skips* its work still exits 0 — a job whose success and whose no-op look identical from outside is telling you nothing.** A scheduler ran green nightly while skipping its main stage on a misread config value, the only trace one skip line in a log nobody opens on a green run. Make every skip state what it skipped and why in the run's own visible output, and confirm a routine works by reading a *reason*, not an exit code: a skip is a finding to triage, not a pass. And when the defect lives inside the mechanism that updates itself (a vendored mount its own maintenance job refreshes, a bootstrap that installs its own successor), the ordinary route can't carry the fix — recognise the self-reference and land the repair out of band rather than waiting for the broken updater.
18	- **The session that designed a judgment stage must not be the one that runs it.** A stage that picks the strongest candidate, ranks a set, or decides what matters has to run in a context that never saw it being built — the designing session knows which candidates it had in mind when it chose the heuristic and will find them again, which is an echo, not judgment. Exercise a freshly-built stage in a subagent whose context starts empty, or leave it to the scheduler. Better, make the clean context **structural rather than remembered**: state it in the task spec as a rule the agent reads every run ("do not load context you were not given — the item's own title, body and discussion are what you have, and they are enough"), so the production path is clean without anyone arranging it.

1	# Working discipline
2	
3	- **Starting any requested change** — begin from the *problem*, not the solution, in any
4	  repository and not just this one. Reach an explicit shared understanding with the owner of the
5	  problem the change is meant to solve **and** agreement that the requested change is the best way
6	  to solve it; a different fix, or none, may serve better.
7	
8	- **Replying to an owner comment** — open with an explicit classification line,
9	  `Comment class: correction | feature | process-change | other`, where `other` covers questions,
10	  approvals and command phrases and a mixed comment names each part. An automation dispatch prompt
11	  is a comment too: class `other`, in your *first* substantive reply rather than at the end of the
12	  run. Put the class **alone on the line** and any explanation on the next one: the line is scanned
13	  for *every* class token on it, so restating the menu declares all of them. A class cannot be taken
14	  back, and a clean re-declaration further down does not override the first.
15	
16	- **Acting on a correction** — you misunderstood something. Repair the shared understanding, then
17	  rework what the misread already touched; the artifact changes as much as the correction demands,
18	  but a correction never adds a new requirement or rule.
19	
20	- **Acting on a feature** — agree on the requirement, record it in the project's requirements
21	  document (its executable spec, where it keeps one), write the test that proves it and watch it
22	  fail, then implement until it passes.
23	
24	- **Acting on a process change** — the owner is changing *how* work is done. Land it as durable
25	  rules in the project's local scope, its own local packs (in Claudinite itself, its packs), routed
26	  through the mechanism promotion ladder (platform setting → hook → check → skill → prose).
27	  Promoting a rule into the shared canon is the growth lifecycle's separate call, not the
28	  interactive session's.
29	
30	- **Choosing what goes on that ladder** — only a rule that constrains *how work is done* and
31	  outlives any one feature; a checkable signature doesn't earn a rule its place. Reject two shapes
32	  outright: a check that asserts particular code exists or still reads a particular way (it pins a
33	  point in time), and a rule derivable from the product's requirements (that is a requirement —
34	  take it to the feature path, the requirements document and the test that proves it).
35	
36	- **Landing a rule anywhere on the ladder** — author the assurance first, the check the future
37	  world must satisfy, execute it and watch it fail, and only then make the fixes that turn it green.
38	  At the prose rung, where no check can carry an in-flight judgment rule, the equivalent step is
39	  showing the corpus doesn't already cover the rule before writing it.
40	
41	- **Building a mechanism for a behavior** — verify against a real run that it isn't already
42	  provided.
43	
44	- **Building release, deploy, versioning or CI plumbing** — look for the shared pack that owns it
45	  first; copying a mechanic from a sibling repo is the tell that it belongs centrally. If no pack
46	  owns it, report the gap rather than author a third copy.
47	
48	- **Finishing a change** — watch it work **now**; never park it on "check tomorrow". What a task
49	  costs is its shelf-life, the time from starting it until everyone can forget about it.
50	
51	- **Changing scheduled or unattended machinery** — force a run now (the scheduler's wake lever, a
52	  `workflow_dispatch`, the fleet-wide force sweep) and watch it to a terminal state rather than wait
53	  for its next natural run.
54	
55	- **Planning a migration** — prefer the design that converges in one forced pass to the one that
56	  trickles across nightly cycles, accept legacy input at the door so nothing has to wait for
57	  stragglers, and drive the stragglers with a standing mechanism rather than a phase someone must
58	  remember to close. Write every phase's code — the cleanup, the destructive tail and every
59	  legacy tolerance's removal included — before asking for approval, and chain each execution step

content.content:
14	- After `git mv`, re-read the file at its **new** path before rewriting it — an editing tool that tracks reads by path treats the moved path as never-seen and silently refuses the write, leaving the file stale (a failure that surfaces much later, far from its cause). When the move and the rewrite share a batch of tool calls, check each result individually; a single refused write is easy to miss in a batch.
15	- To exclude a directory's own files from a reference search, filter by file **path**, not `grep -v` on line content: `grep -rn foo/bar | grep -v foo/bar/` (meant to drop the directory's own files) *also* drops every legitimate full-path reference elsewhere, silently undercounting. Exclude by pathspec instead — `git grep -n foo/bar -- . ':(exclude)foo/bar'` — which filters on which file is searched, not on what each matching line happens to contain.

---
name: repo-text-sweeps
description: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
---

# Text & file manipulation

Sweeping across a **merge** — git's rename detection, references that break with no conflict — is [git-github-advanced](../../../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md)'s "Merging across a file relocation".

- When you relocate a file's *content or responsibility* into a new home — folding a doc into a pack, moving a function to another module, absorbing a routine into a skill — the original is now **redundant surface**, and reducing it to a tombstone stub (`# retired — see X`) is not finishing the job: the stub still costs a read, drifts from its replacement, and misleads anyone who lands on it. Delete the emptied original in the *same* change, and treat "did this move make anything else dead?" as a standing question after every restructure — the source you copied *from* is the first suspect. Don't wait to be told a leftover is redundant; a relocation that leaves two homes for one thing isn't done.
- When renaming `foo/` → `bar/foo/`, a naive repo-wide string-replace of `foo/` → `bar/foo/` causes two silent corruptions: files already under the target namespace double-prefix (`bar/foo/file` → `bar/bar/foo/file`), and external URLs containing the string `foo/` get rewritten. Scope the replace to only internal path strings that need it, or do the replace then make a targeted post-pass reverting matches inside URLs and already-correct paths.
- A grep/sed rename pass over a path (`foo/bar/baz.js`) won't match it when built from `path.join` segments (`path.join(__dirname, "foo", "bar", "baz.js")`) or wrapped across a line in a comment — those references survive the rewrite and break only at run time. After a mechanical path-rename pass, also search for the path's individual segment tokens and run the test suite; the test suite, not the grep, surfaces a missed reference.
- An ordered specific→catch-all path rewrite can half-convert a reference the specific rule's trailing slash missed. Renaming `old/sub/` → `new/leaf/` with a slash-anchored rule (`s#old/sub/#new/leaf/#`) plus a catch-all for the parent (`s#old/#new/#`), a reference *without* the trailing slash (`path.join(root, "old/sub")`, a bare `git add old/sub`, a prose mention) escapes the specific rule, and the catch-all then rewrites only its **parent** — `old/sub` → `new/sub`, not `new/leaf` — a half-converted path that breaks at run time, not at the rewrite. Match both the slashed and bare forms, then grep the bare-dir form (at a quote / paren / line-end) and run the tests.
- After `git mv`, re-read the file at its **new** path before rewriting it — an editing tool that tracks reads by path treats the moved path as never-seen and silently refuses the write, leaving the file stale (a failure that surfaces much later, far from its cause). When the move and the rewrite share a batch of tool calls, check each result individually; a single refused write is easy to miss in a batch.

- To exclude vendored, synced, or generated files from a **structural** check that walks a tree (an orphan/reachability scan, a doc audit, a lint), derive the file set from git's tracked list (e.g. `git ls-files`) rather than a filesystem walk with a hardcoded path to skip — it can't desync when the artifact moves, and it stays correct when a new ignored directory appears. (Sibling of the pathspec-exclude rule above: that one separates a directory from its own files within a search; this one separates owned content from vendored/generated content.)
- A zero-hit grep proves absence only at the case you searched. Code normalizes tokens away from prose case — an uppercase data table (`'KNEW'`), a SCREAMING_SNAKE constant, a lowercased slug — so a case-sensitive `grep knew` finds nothing and reads as "not in the codebase" while the entry sits right there, and a conclusion built on that phantom absence compounds. Before concluding a token is absent, re-run with `-i`; when history should have touched it, `git log -S<token>` is the cross-check that catches the miss.

`commit.gpgsign = true` signs ordinary commits but does not apply to `git merge` — each merge produces an unsigned commit even with signing fully configured. In a repo that enforces commit verification, this requires a fix-up after the fact. Cover merges proactively: either pass `-S` to every `git merge` call, or set `merge.gpgsign = true` globally so merges are signed the same way commits are.

## When access is scoped to an explicit repo list, query per-repo — never an org/user-wide search

A broad call (e.g. `search_repositories` with `org:X`, or any list/search tool that takes no repo argument) returns every repo the token can see, not just an allowed subset — filtering the result afterward doesn't undo the fact that disallowed repos' data was already pulled into the call. When operating under a repo allowlist, scope every call explicitly instead: pass the specific `owner`/`repo` params, or anchor the query to `repo:owner/name`, one call per repo in the allowlist rather than one broad call filtered after the fact.

A session scoped to a **single** repo hits the same boundary from the other side: a call naming a *different* repo is denied outright, not merely filtered. Before spending a call rediscovering that denial, check what repo the session is actually scoped to — and look for the answer in what you already have. An issue or PR body that references the other repo often already carries its own self-description of the state you were about to go fetch.

## `search_code`'s index can lag — don't trust it alone to enumerate a population

Reconnaissance across many repos (which ones reference X, which ones need a given change) often reaches for `search_code`, but its index is not the source of truth for coverage: it can silently undercount, missing repos that genuinely match. Where you have a way to enumerate the true candidate set directly — fetching each candidate's own file, walking a known roster — cross-check `search_code`'s result against that before trusting it as complete; one fleet-wide sweep found only 3 of 11 actually-affected repos through `search_code` alone.

## Write access scoped to one repo doesn't license routing around the boundary for a fix that belongs elsewhere

A session's push/write access is commonly scoped to a single repo, even when it can *read* others (a cloned dependency, a monorepo neighbour, an upstream project). Finding a genuine bug in a repo you can only read is not license to hunt for a way to push there anyway — that scoping is a deliberate boundary, not an oversight to route around, and it doesn't move for a good reason. Finish and verify the fix in a scratch clone of the repo that owns it, then attach it as a diff/patch to an issue in the repo you *can* write to, carrying what you verified — so a session with the right scope can `git apply` it and land it properly reviewed.

that can be denied (403 through the proxy) even when ordinary git operations against the same repo
work fine. When a tarball fetch is refused, reach for `git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>`
instead of retrying the download or widening the allowlist — it goes through the allowed host and
yields the same tree.

@@ -21,6 +21,10 @@ To post a **status update** on an issue (the lifecycle's "update the issue's sta
 
 Never re-arm on a loop hoping the answer changes — observed runs answered "unstable" then "clean" seconds later with nothing changed in between, and one spent ~6 minutes of a 13-minute budget circling a single PR without merging it.
 
+## After a bulk sweep, subscribe every PR it leaves open — not a sample
+
+A fleet-wide or bulk sweep can leave many PRs open at once; subscribing to only some of them means the rest get no activity signal at all, so detecting their merges falls back to repeated re-polling — real API and wall-clock cost, spent on state that never changes between polls. The subscribed few, by contrast, report back the instant the owner acts. Call the PR-activity subscription on **every** PR the run leaves open, not just the ones that look interesting.
+
 ## Don't prune a `.gitignore` section in the same commit that deletes what produced its artifacts
 
 Removing a toolchain invites tidying away its ignore rules alongside it — but the artifacts it already produced are usually still sitting untracked in the worktree (`__pycache__/` from an earlier run, `build/` from an earlier build). The moment those rules go, the next `git add -A` sweeps the junk *into* the commit that was supposed to remove it, and nothing complains: the commit is valid and the tests still pass. Delete (or `git clean`) the artifacts first, then drop their ignore lines. And after any bulk `git add -A`, read `git diff --cached --stat` — staged additions are exactly what a clean `git status` stops telling you about.
@@ -40,6 +44,7 @@ There's no cost to a branch carrying many commits when the project uses a **squa
 
 - **When a rebase or a review round drops part of a branch, amend the commit message in the same step** — then read it back against `git show --stat` before merging. Under a squash merge the branch's commit body *becomes* `main`'s permanent record, while the explanation of what was dropped, if it lives in a PR comment, is not carried by the squash at all. A commit describing a change to files it never touched sends the next reader of `git log -- <path>` hunting for work that isn't there.
 
+- **When a Stop-hook or CI finding names its own fix as a plain amend, take that fix — don't reach for history-rewriting machinery instead.** A check whose failure message already says "amend the latest commit" is answered by exactly that; scripting a `filter-branch`/rewrite pass across every prior commit to backdate the fix into each one is needless extra risk (a wrong regex, a bad force-push) for no benefit over the one-line remedy the finding already gave you.
 - Don't rewrite published/shared history to satisfy a tooling or authorship check (e.g. a hook flagging "unverified" commits): only amend your own un-pushed branch commits. 15	
16	# Testing practices
17	
18	A consuming repo's own test *mechanics* — runner, layout, which suites exist — are its own docs'; CI-trigger rules and the `GITHUB_TOKEN` workflow-recursion gotcha are [git-github-advanced](../../../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md)'s.
19	
20	<<<<<<< HEAD
21	- See a test fail before you trust it: write it red before the fix (green after), or break what it guards and watch it go red. A test that has never failed proves nothing. For a **refusal/negative** test — one asserting a guard yields *nothing* — the write-it-red-first branch is unavailable: the pre-change code also yielded nothing, so the test passes from birth and proves nothing. See-it-fail there **must** be the second method — mutate the new guard (weaken it), watch the test bite, then restore it. Restore with `git checkout -- <file>` (or `git stash`) taken at the moment of mutating — never a `.bak` copy saved earlier, which predates whatever else you edited in between and silently discards that intervening work. If the case you're triggering reads **staged** content (a check that scans `git diff --cached` or otherwise needs the violation `git add`-ed to fire), a bare `git checkout -- <file>` restores from the **index** — which still holds the staged mutation — so the "restore" is a no-op; use `git checkout HEAD -- <file>` (or `git reset` first) to actually clear it.

23	- See a test fail before you trust it: write it red before the fix (green after), or break what it guards and watch it go red. A test that has never failed proves nothing. For a **refusal/negative** test — one asserting a guard yields *nothing* — the write-it-red-first branch is unavailable: the pre-change code also yielded nothing, so the test passes from birth and proves nothing. See-it-fail there **must** be the second method — mutate the new guard (weaken it), watch the test bite, then restore it. Restore with `git checkout -- <file>` (or `git stash`) taken at the moment of mutating — never a `.bak` copy saved earlier, which predates whatever else you edited in between and silently discards that intervening work. If the mutation was staged (`git add`ed) rather than left in the working tree — e.g. to prove a check fires on a violation about to be committed — `git checkout -- <file>` restores from the **index**, which now holds the mutation itself, so the "restore" silently leaves it in place; use `git checkout HEAD -- <file>` (or `git reset` first) instead.
24	>>>>>>> 6b352e8c (Promote lessons from ClaudiniteWebsite, MissingBulbWebsite, Shepherd, WIP)
25	- A mechanism meant to survive a retry, re-queue, or hand-off needs a test that calls it twice, not once. A suite of single-call tests stays green while the multi-call case corrupts state — the double-call is what a real retry, requeue, or hand-off actually does. When the mechanism arbitrates by identity (a claim, a lock), the second call must come from a **different actor**: a single actor retrying its own stale claim can't expose an identity-masked race, since it still recognizes its own claim as valid.
26	- A simulator of a stateful mechanism must advance state only where the real engine's code actually leaves a mark — never wherever the rule's stated description says a transition happens. A sim that fires on every event matching the rule's *intent* is correct by construction against that rule and blind to exactly the silent paths where the real implementation and the rule have quietly diverged — which is where a genuine bug usually lives. Read the real engine's code for what it *writes*, and model that.

- A mechanism meant to survive a retry, re-queue, or hand-off needs a test that calls it twice, not once. A suite of single-call tests stays green while the multi-call case corrupts state — the double-call is what a real retry, requeue, or hand-off actually does. When the mechanism arbitrates by identity (a claim, a lock), the second call must come from a **different actor**: a single actor retrying its own stale claim can't expose an identity-masked race, since it still recognizes its own claim as valid.

- A simulator of a stateful mechanism must advance state only where the real engine's code actually leaves a mark — never wherever the rule's stated description says a transition happens. A sim that fires on every event matching the rule's *intent* is correct by construction against that rule and blind to exactly the silent paths where the real implementation and the rule have quietly diverged — which is where a genuine bug usually lives. Read the real engine's code for what it *writes*, and model that.

- Before trusting a new transform/normalizer, run it over the *real existing corpus* it will process, not just hand-picked test inputs — the live data exposes edge cases your examples won't. Relatedly, prefer a generic structural rule over a hand-maintained list of special cases: the enumerated list needs per-instance upkeep and silently has gaps, while a rule keyed on structure (e.g. "a known registry label under any 2-letter ccTLD") covers the whole class at once.  - Render a UI *image* golden with the engine that matches the surface, and prefer the deterministic one. Match the engine to the surface; never reshape the product to fit the rasterizer. (A rasterized popup golden works only because the popup was authored flexbox-only — the moment a surface needs grid/vars/widgets, it needs a browser.) Since the browser goldens aren't gate-able bit-exact and a runner may lack the browser, let those cases **self-skip** where it's absent so the deterministic cases still gate.

--- a/packs/claudinite-growth/skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md
+++ b/packs/claudinite-growth/skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md
@@ -24,6 +24,7 @@ description: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agent
 - A `[Merge Without Review]` security warning on a task's own unattended merge is expected, not a finding to escalate — adjudicate it in one step. When a task's declared delivery policy is auto-merge and its target's checks require no human approval (or the arm is rejected `clean status` and a direct merge is the sanctioned path), the harness still flags the completion with a security warning because no human approval appears in the transcript — that is the harness reporting the *shape* of the action, not evaluating whether it was licensed. Confirm the task's declared delivery policy and its outcome ceiling permit the merge, then converge normally; escalating every occurrence to human review would wedge a routine that is designed to merge unattended.
 - A background subagent dispatch shares the parent's working directory unless isolated, so the parent's own end-of-session checks can misread the subagent's activity as its own. Without `isolation: "worktree"`, a background agent runs in the *same* checkout as the session that spawned it, so while it's running: its uncommitted WIP can look like the parent's own dirty diff to a git-status-based finding, and if it switches branches (e.g. checking out another branch to inspect or fix it), a check that reads the current branch now reads *its* branch, not the parent's. Before diagnosing such a finding as your own — one naming "the branch" or "the commit", or unreferenced/uncommitted changes — check whether a background agent is still running; if a mid-dispatch finding names a branch other than the one you were assigned, switch back to your own branch to clear it rather than treating the finding as real.
 - **Parallel background agents that each dump external content to disk need a collision-proof filename, not a shared generic one.** Subagents dispatched from one session share its scratchpad directory, so a fleet of them each told (or defaulting) to write the same generic path — a bare `log.jsonl`, `out.txt` — race on it: one agent's write can land mid-read by another, producing a truncated or mixed-content file with no error from either side. Give each agent's output a name that can't collide with its siblings' — the source item's own filename, or the agent's own session id — never a shared default.
+- **Once a source is delegated to a background subagent, don't also mine or duplicate-analyze it yourself while waiting.** Racing ahead with your own read of the same file the subagent owns wastes its entire run when it comes back with the same answer, and produces nothing when it doesn't; either wait with no tool call, or spend the interim on work no subagent already owns. And if you catch a flawed prompt moments after dispatching — a wrong path, an unfilled placeholder — send a **follow-up message to resume that same agent**, never a brand-new dispatch over the identical source: a redispatch runs a full second pass in parallel with the first, at full cost, even when the original would have handled it fine on its own.
 
 ## Structuring a routine as prose + scripts

25	- A background subagent dispatch shares the parent's working directory unless isolated, so the parent's own end-of-session checks can misread the subagent's activity as its own. Without `isolation: "worktree"`, a background agent runs in the *same* checkout as the session that spawned it, so while it's running: its uncommitted WIP can look like the parent's own dirty diff to a git-status-based finding, and if it switches branches (e.g. checking out another branch to inspect or fix it), a check that reads the current branch now reads *its* branch, not the parent's. Before diagnosing such a finding as your own — one naming "the branch" or "the commit", or unreferenced/uncommitted changes — check whether a background agent is still running; if a mid-dispatch finding names a branch other than the one you were assigned, switch back to your own branch to clear it rather than treating the finding as real. Never amend a subagent's already-pushed commit, and never relay a "fix" instruction built around a check that doesn't exist as described — both act on a misdiagnosis instead of correcting it. And if switching back (or an amend) is itself refused by the environment's own permission classifier, don't retry or force it: a live subagent is still using the shared checkout, and the branch — and the false-positive noise with it — reverts to yours on its own the moment the subagent finishes.
26	- **Before concluding a subagent whose handle went unreachable left no progress, check every place its output could have landed — not just git state and the dispatch's own PR comments.** A subagent that hits something worth escalating may record that as a filed tracker issue rather than a commit; a recovery check that reads only local git log and the dispatch PR's comments can miss it entirely, read "nothing survived," and relaunch a duplicate investigation that reproduces — and re-files — the same finding.
27	- **A lost subagent's handle going unreachable is not evidence it made no progress — check every channel it could have written to, not just git.** A subagent whose process is interrupted or restarted mid-task can have already produced real output through a side channel (filing a tracking issue, say) moments before going silent. A recovery check that reads only git log/status and a dispatch PR's own comments will read that as "nothing survived" and relaunch a fresh subagent from a from-scratch briefing — which re-investigates the same ground and produces a duplicate. Before asserting "no progress" in a relaunch briefing, also search for anything the lost subagent may have filed (issues, comments), not just commits.
28	- **Don't perform a dispatched subagent's work yourself before its result is actually in hand.** Backgrounding a subagent to do X and then, before its completion notification (or your own scheduled wakeup) arrives, independently doing X yourself makes the subagent's run entirely redundant the moment it does report back. Once you've stated a wait-for-subagent plan, actually wait — check what its notification says before taking the action it was dispatched to take.
29	- **Parallel background agents that each dump external content to disk need a collision-proof filename, not a shared generic one.** Subagents dispatched from one session share its scratchpad directory, so a fleet of them each told (or defaulting) to write the same generic path — a bare `log.jsonl`, `out.txt` — race on it: one agent's write can land mid-read by another, producing a truncated or mixed-content file with no error from either side. Give each agent's output a name that can't collide with its siblings' — the source item's own filename, or the agent's own session id — never a shared default.
30	<<<<<<< HEAD
31	- **Once a source is delegated to a background subagent, don't also mine or duplicate-analyze it yourself while waiting.** Racing ahead with your own read of the same file the subagent owns wastes its entire run when it comes back with the same answer, and produces nothing when it doesn't; either wait with no tool call, or spend the interim on work no subagent already owns. And if you catch a flawed prompt moments after dispatching — a wrong path, an unfilled placeholder — send a **follow-up message to resume that same agent**, never a brand-new dispatch over the identical source: a redispatch runs a full second pass in parallel with the first, at full cost, even when the original would have handled it fine on its own.

Wait on the dispatched result (idle, or genuinely independent work) rather than shadowing its read.

Without `isolation: "worktree"`, a background agent runs in the *same* checkout as the session that spawned it, so while it's running: its uncommitted WIP can look like the parent's own dirty diff to a git-status-based finding, and if it switches branches (e.g. checking out another branch to inspect or fix it), a check that reads the current branch now reads *its* branch, not the parent's. Before diagnosing such a finding as your own — one naming "the branch" or "the commit", or unreferenced/uncommitted changes — check whether a background agent is still running; if a mid-dispatch finding names a branch other than the one you were assigned, switch back to your own branch to clear it rather than treating the finding as real. Never amend a subagent's already-pushed commit, and never relay a "fix" instruction built around a check that doesn't exist as described — both act on a misdiagnosis instead of correcting it. And if switching back (or an amend) is itself refused by the environment's own permission classifier, don't retry or force it: a live subagent is still using the shared checkout, and the branch — and the false-positive noise with it — reverts to yours on its own the moment the subagent finishes.
- **Before concluding a subagent whose handle went unreachable left no progress, check every place its output could have landed — not just git state and the dispatch's own PR comments.** A subagent that hits something worth escalating may record that as a filed tracker issue rather than a commit; a recovery check that reads only local git log and the dispatch PR's comments can miss it entirely, read "nothing survived," and relaunch a duplicate investigation that reproduces — and re-files — the same finding.
- **A lost subagent's handle going unreachable is not evidence it made no progress — check every channel it could have written to, not just git.** A subagent whose process is interrupted or restarted mid-task can have already produced real output through a side channel (filing a tracking issue, say) moments before going silent. A recovery check that reads only git log/status and a dispatch PR's own comments will read that as "nothing survived" and relaunch a fresh subagent from a from-scratch briefing — which re-investigates the same ground and produces a duplicate. Before asserting "no progress" in a relaunch briefing, also search for anything the lost subagent may have filed (issues, comments), not just commits.
- **Don't perform a dispatched subagent's work yourself before its result is actually in hand.** Backgrounding a subagent to do X and then, before its completion notification (or your own scheduled wakeup) arrives, independently doing X yourself makes the subagent's run entirely redundant the moment it does report back. Once you've stated a wait-for-subagent plan, actually wait — check what its notification says before taking the action it was dispatched to take.
- **Parallel background agents that each dump external content to disk need a collision-proof filename, not a shared generic one.** Subagents dispatched from one session share its scratchpad directory, so a fleet of them each told (or defaulting) to write the same generic path — a bare `log.jsonl`, `out.txt` — race on it: one agent's write can land mid-read by another, producing a truncated or mixed-content file with no error from either side. Give each agent's output a name that can't collide with its siblings' — the source item's own filename, or the agent's own session id — never a shared default.

And if you catch a flawed prompt moments after dispatching — a wrong path, an unfilled placeholder — send a **follow-up message to resume that same agent**, never a brand-new dispatch over the identical source: a redispatch runs a full second pass in parallel with the first, at full cost, even when the original would have handled it fine on its own.

Wait on the dispatched result (idle, or genuinely independent work) rather than shadowing its read.

Before asserting "no progress survived" and relaunching a fresh subagent from scratch, also search issues for anything the lost one may have filed; skipping that step is how a relaunch re-investigates the same finding and files a duplicate.

# core — working with Claudinite itself

- **Reading a rule, check or skill that arrived from Claudinite** — it is vendored, under
  `.claudinite/shared/`, and the update flows replace that whole tree. Never edit anything there:
  change it in the canon, or carry the difference in this repo's own `.claudinite/local/packs/`.

- **Finding a mounted skill, or following a link from inside one you already loaded** — a canon
  skill lives at `.claudinite/shared/packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`; there is no flat
  `.claudinite/shared/skills/`. When the `Skill` tool announces a per-session flat "base directory"
  (e.g. `.claude/skills/<name>/`) that holds only that one `SKILL.md`, any relative link the
  skill's own text carries (to a sibling doc, a sibling skill) was written for its real home and
  dangles from that announced base — resolve such links against the canon path instead.

- **Finding which check enforces a given rule** — read that pack's own
  `.claudinite/shared/packs/<pack>/declared-checks.json` directly rather than grepping the engine's
  check-runner source. A declared check is data-driven config, not keyword-searchable script text,
  so the pack's own manifest is the fast path to its id, description and failure message.

- **Wanting a pack's rules to apply here** — declare its id in `.claudinite-settings.json`. Nothing
  activates by being mounted, fingerprinted or present on disk, so a pack whose files you can see
  but whose id is undeclared contributes no prose, no checks, no skills and no tasks.

- **Renaming or removing a pack's declaration** — re-run
  `node .claudinite/shared/engine/converge-wiring.mjs <owner/repo> --badges` in the same
  change. The README's `<!-- claudinite:packs -->` badge row is a one-time seed the update flow
  deliberately never re-derives on its own, so a declaration change made outside the `adopt-pack`
  skill (which already runs this) leaves the row silently stale — surfacing only later as a
  blocking `reference-integrity` finding, sometimes on the *second* rename of the same pack.

- **Adding a pack** — run the `adopt-pack` skill, which declares it, asks its adoption questions,
  re-vendors and scaffolds. Never hand-copy a pack's content into the repo.

- **Setting a project up on Claudinite for the first time** — the `adopt-claudinite` skill.

- **Deciding which pack owns a lesson** — read `packs/directory.GENERATED.md`, the catalog of
  *every* canon pack, never the mounted subset: the mount holds only what this repo declares, so the
  pack that owns the territory may be absent and invisible. When the owning pack is merely too

# core

Claudinite's own surface in a repo that runs it: the vendored mount, the declaration that activates a
pack, adopting Claudinite and adopting a pack, and the contract every scheduled task is written to.

**Mandatory.** `basics` `requires` this pack, so the closure vendors its content and materializes its
declaration wherever a declaration is written; the one-time `core-seed` migration record declares it
into members that already exist. Removing the entry is not an opt-out — it is drift, and `claudinite-lifecycle-declared`
reports it.

## Rules (`RULES.md`)

| Rule | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reading a rule that arrived from Claudinite | high | correctness | prose: 43 words + check (`claudinite-isolation`) |
| Finding a mounted skill's real path | medium | complexity | prose: 81 words |
| Finding which check enforces a rule | medium | complexity | prose: 48 words |
| Wanting a pack's rules to apply here | high | correctness | prose: 47 words + check (`claudinite-lifecycle-declared`) |
| Renaming or removing a pack's declaration | high | correctness | prose: 73 words |
| Adding a pack | medium | complexity | prose: 27 words |
| Setting a project up on Claudinite | medium | complexity | prose: 15 words |
| Deciding which pack owns a lesson | medium | complexity | prose: 59 words |
| Judging whether Claudinite is current here | medium | correctness | prose: 51 words |
| Answering "why did the mount not update" | medium | correctness | prose: 39 words |
